Imagine holding a globe of the Earth. Now imagine slicing it like an orange — not across the middle, but from the top (North Pole) to the bottom (South Pole). Each slice you make would be a thin, wedge-shaped section of the Earth. The curved edge on the surface of each such slice — a line running from the North Pole straight down to the South Pole — is called a line of longitude, or a meridian.

Longitude is a way of measuring how far east or west a particular location on Earth is, using these imaginary lines as a reference system.
Why Do We Need It?

The Earth is a sphere. To describe the exact position of any point on a sphere, you need two pieces of information — just like how to describe a point on a flat grid you need both an X value and a Y value. For Earth:

  • Latitude tells you how far north or south you are.
  • Longitude tells you how far east or west you are.

Together, latitude and longitude form a coordinate system that can pinpoint any location on Earth with complete precision.
The Starting Line: The Prime Meridian

To measure "how far east or west," you need a starting point — a reference line to measure from. That line is called the Prime Meridian, and it is assigned a longitude of 0° (zero degrees).

The Prime Meridian is an internationally agreed-upon imaginary line that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole, passing through Greenwich, a town in London, England. This choice was made historically (in 1884) and has been used worldwide ever since.

Everything to the east of this line is called East longitude, and everything to the west is called West longitude.
How Longitude Is Measured

Longitude is measured in degrees (°), using the center of the Earth as the point from which the angle is calculated.

Think of it this way: if you stood at the center of the Earth and looked outward, the angle between the Prime Meridian (0°) and the line going to your chosen location on the surface — measured either eastward or westward — is that location's longitude.

  • The Prime Meridian itself is 0° longitude.
  • Moving eastward from it, longitude increases from 0° to 180° East.
  • Moving westward from it, longitude increases from 0° to 180° West.
  • The 180° line (called the International Date Line, roughly) is on the exact opposite side of the Earth from the Prime Meridian. Going east or going west, you meet it at the same line — so 180° East and 180° West are the same line.

This means the full range of longitude values is: 180° West → 0° → 180° East, covering the entire Earth.
How Degrees Are Further Divided

Because degrees are large units, longitude can also be expressed in smaller units for greater precision:

  • Each degree (°) is divided into 60 minutes (′)
  • Each minute is divided into 60 seconds (″)

So a longitude might be written as: 73° 56′ 18″ E — meaning 73 degrees, 56 minutes, and 18 seconds east of the Prime Meridian. This level of precision can pin a location to within a few meters on the Earth's surface.

In modern GPS systems, the minutes and seconds are often replaced with decimal degrees instead — e.g., 73.938° E — which means the same thing but is easier for computers to work with.
What Lines of Longitude Look Like

All lines of longitude are:

  • Equal in length — every meridian runs from the North Pole to the South Pole, so they are all the same length (unlike lines of latitude, which shrink as you go toward the poles).
  • Shaped like half-circles — each one is a semicircle on the globe's surface.
  • Converging at the poles — all lines of longitude meet at both the North Pole and the South Pole, like the segments of an orange meeting at the top and bottom.
  • Farthest apart at the Equator — the distance between two neighboring lines of longitude is widest at the Equator and shrinks to zero at the poles.
Reading a Longitude Value

When you see a longitude value, here's how to read it:

  • 0° → You're on the Prime Meridian (through London).
  • 90° E → You're one-quarter of the way around the Earth going east (roughly near Bangladesh/Bhutan).
  • 90° W → You're one-quarter of the way around going west (roughly through the central United States).
  • 180° → You're on the opposite side of the Earth from the Prime Meridian (in the middle of the Pacific Ocean).

For reference, India sits roughly between 68° E and 97° E longitude, which is why your clocks are ahead of London by 5 hours and 30 minutes.
Longitude and Time Zones

This brings up one of the most practical uses of longitude: time zones.

The Earth takes 24 hours to rotate 360°. So it rotates:

360° ÷ 24 hours = 15° per hour

This means every 15° of longitude you move east, the local time is one hour ahead, and every 15° you move west, it is one hour behind.

This is why time zones exist and why they follow longitude lines roughly. For example, India Standard Time (IST) is UTC+5:30 because India is approximately 82.5° East of the Prime Meridian (82.5 ÷ 15 = 5.5 hours = 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich).
Longitude vs. Latitude — A Quick Contrast

These two are often confused, so here's the clearest way to tell them apart:

LongitudeLatitude
Direction measuredEast–WestNorth–South
Lines runNorth–South (top to bottom)East–West (side to side)
Range0° to 180° E or W0° to 90° N or S
All lines equal length?YesNo
Lines meet?Yes, at the polesNo, they are parallel

A helpful memory trick: "Lat" is flat — lines of latitude are horizontal (flat) bands wrapping around the Earth like rings. Lines of longitude, on the other hand, are long — they run the full length of the Earth from pole to pole.
Real-World Uses of Longitude

Longitude is not just an academic concept — it is used everywhere:

  • Navigation: Ships, aircraft, and GPS devices use longitude (together with latitude) to determine their exact position anywhere on Earth.
  • Mapping: Every map and atlas uses a grid of latitude and longitude lines to locate places accurately.
  • Time zones: As explained, the world's time zones are built directly on the concept of longitude.
  • Satellite systems: Satellites in geostationary orbit (like communication and weather satellites) are positioned and identified by their longitude above the Equator.
  • Surveying and construction: Large-scale engineering projects use longitude to establish precise locations.
  • Astronomy: Longitude is also adapted for use in celestial coordinate systems to locate objects in the sky.
Summary

Longitude is a measurement that tells you how far east or west a point on Earth is from the Prime Meridian — an imaginary reference line running from pole to pole through Greenwich, England. It is expressed in degrees, ranging from 0° at the Prime Meridian to 180° in either direction. Lines of longitude run vertically from pole to pole, and all of them meet at the poles. Together with latitude, longitude gives every location on Earth a unique, precise address. It also forms the mathematical basis for the world's time zones.
